title: "Marginal distributions"

The [joint-distribution definition](joint-probability.qmd#definition) assigns
mass to paired recipient and theme lengths. A [**marginal distribution**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) removes
one coordinate by summing over all its possible values. The retained
coordinate's frequencies remain, but every fact about which values co-occurred
is discarded.

We derive each marginal by summing the [joint PMF](joint-probability.qmd) over the unwanted coordinate, verify the operation on the dative table, and then identify exactly which pairing information cannot be recovered afterward. A marginal PMF assigns each retained value the total mass of every pair containing that value.

## Marginalization

For recipient length $R$ and theme length $T$,

$$
p_R(r)=\sum_t p_{R,T}(r,t),
\qquad
p_T(t)=\sum_r p_{R,T}(r,t).
$$

Each marginal normalizes:

$$
\sum_r p_R(r)=1,
\qquad
\sum_t p_T(t)=1.
$$

Marginalization forgets the pairing but not the frequency of the retained variable.

For a joint density, summation becomes integration:

$$
f_R(r)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dt,
\qquad
f_T(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dr.
$$

Marginalization should not be confused with conditioning. When $p_T(t)>0$,

$$
p_{R\mid T}(r\mid t)=\frac{p_{R,T}(r,t)}{p_T(t)},
$$

which fixes one value and renormalizes instead of summing it out.

For a concrete row sum, 2,228 tokens have recipient length one. Summing all <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
joint cells with $r=1$ gives

$$
p_R(1)=\sum_t p_{R,T}(1,t)=\frac{2228}{3263}=0.682807. % dqr-allow: empirical-answer
$$
<!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

Conditioning at, say, $T=2$ would instead retain only the $t=2$ column and
divide its cells by that column total.

```{r}
#| label: dative-marginal-pmfs
library(ggplot2)

dative <- read.csv(
  "data/english-dative/dative-alternation.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("", "NA")
)
joint <- as.data.frame(table(
  recipient = dative$recipient_length_words,
  theme = dative$theme_length_words
), responseName = "count")
joint$recipient <- as.integer(as.character(joint$recipient))
joint$theme <- as.integer(as.character(joint$theme))
joint$probability <- joint$count / nrow(dative)

recipient_margin <- aggregate(cbind(count, probability) ~ recipient,
                              data = joint, FUN = sum)
names(recipient_margin)[1] <- "value"
recipient_margin$constituent <- "recipient"

theme_margin <- aggregate(cbind(count, probability) ~ theme,
                          data = joint, FUN = sum)
names(theme_margin)[1] <- "value"
theme_margin$constituent <- "theme"

margins <- rbind(recipient_margin, theme_margin)
direct_recipient <- prop.table(table(dative$recipient_length_words))

stopifnot(
  abs(sum(recipient_margin$probability) - 1) < 1e-12,
  abs(sum(theme_margin$probability) - 1) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(recipient_margin$probability - as.numeric(direct_recipient))) < 1e-12
)

aggregate(cbind(expectation = value * probability,
                second_moment = value^2 * probability) ~ constituent,
          data = margins, FUN = sum)
```

The empirical marginal expectations can be computed either from the row-level measurements or from their PMFs:

$$
\mathbb{E}[R]=\sum_r r\,p_R(r),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[T]=\sum_t t\,p_T(t).
$$

In this table, those means are `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(dative$recipient_length_words))` recipient words and `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(dative$theme_length_words))` theme words.

```{r}
#| label: plot-dative-margins
#| fig-cap: "Marginal empirical PMFs obtained by summing the dative joint distribution."
ggplot(margins, aes(value, probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey55", width = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~constituent, scales = "free_x", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Constituent length (words)", y = "Empirical probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The plots retain the different supports and tail shapes. They do not show whether a long recipient occurred with a long or short theme; that information existed only in the joint distribution.

## Check your understanding

1. Marginalize `joint` with `rowsum()` or matrix operations and compare the result.
2. Compute each marginal [variance](variance-and-covariance.qmd) from the PMF, using the expected squared distance from its marginal mean.
3. Why can two datasets have identical marginal plots but different joint plots?
4. Which marginal has the longer observed support?
5. A student sums the $T=2$ column and then rescales its cells to one. Has the
   student marginalized or conditioned?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Summing `joint` over theme columns reproduces `recipient_margin`, and summing over recipient rows reproduces the theme margin; both normalized margins sum to one. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The PMFs give $\operatorname{Var}[R]=4.274507$ and $\operatorname{Var}[T]=18.986650$ words squared. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Identical marginals retain the same separate value frequencies but can arise from different pairings, which produce different joint distributions. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Theme length has the longer observed support: 36 distinct values from 1 to 46, versus 20 recipient values from 1 to 31. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The student has conditioned on $T=2$. Marginalization would sum over every
   theme value and retain only recipient length.

</details>

Marginalization sums out one coordinate, preserving its one-variable
frequencies while discarding the original pairings. Conditioning does something
different: it fixes and renormalizes rather than summing out. The
[conditional-independence page](conditional-independence.qmd) asks whether two
dative annotations factorize after modality is held fixed.
